ABOUT THE BOOK

 

 

In chapter one, you will learn to know the properties and events of each control in a Windows Visual C# applications. You need to learn and know in order to be more familiar when applying them to some desktop applications in this book.

 

In chapter two, you will build Throwing Fire program. This program can be played by two human players or human player versus computer. You will use 12 labels, a large control panel, and three control buttons on the form. In the control panel, a smaller panel with two group box controls and a button control are placed. In the first group box, you will use 2 radio buttons; in the second box group, place 4 radio buttons. Next, two timer controls are added to the project. All label controls are used for titles and provide scoring and game information. The large panel (Panel1) is the playing field. Three button controls are used to start / stop a program, set options, and exit the program. One timer control is used to control game animation and another is used to represent the computer's decision process. The second control panel (Panel2) is used to select game options. One group box contains radio buttons which are used to select number of players. A group box contains radio buttons to select the level of difficulty of the game, when playing against a computer. A small button is used to close the options panel. The default properties are set for one-player games with the easiest game difficulty.

 

In chapter three, you will build Roasted Duck Delivery simulation. In this simulation, a number of decisions are needed. The basic idea is to read the order by incoming telephone and tell the delivery scooter to go to the location of the order. You also need to make sure that you always provide a roasted duck ready to be transported by the delivery scooter. The delivery area is a 20 by 20 square grid. The more roasted duck is sold, the more profit it gets. The panel control on the left side of the form contains the delivery grid. On the upper right are group boxes with two label controls to display the time or hour and sale results. The computer monitor (in a picture box) displays order and delivery status using a list box and label control. Another group box contains a roasting oven when the roasted ducks are displayed using eight picture box controls. Two button controls on the group box control the operation of the oven. Group boxes under the oven show how many ducks are ready to be delivered and how many are in the delivery scooter (a button control is to load the roasted duck into the scooter). The two button controls beneath are used to start/pause the game and to stop the game or exit the game. In the area under the form there are several timers for controlling a number of aspects in the program. The delivery grid consists of 400 label controls on 20 rows (marked with numbers) and 20 columns (marked with letters). Here, you will learn how to place controls on a form (or panel in this case) using code (when the program runs, not when designing the form). This mechanism can save time designing the form.

 

In chapter four, you will build a Drone Simulation. In this simulation, you control both vertical and horizontal thrusters to maneuver the ride to the landing pad. You will adjust the landing speed so that it is slow enough so that no accident occurs. You build the form in two stages, the first stage creates two option group boxes, and then the second stage uses both those group boxes as landing controls. Two control panels are placed on the left side of the form: one panel for drawing and another panel for the edge. On the right side of the form, place the two group control boxes. In the first group box, five radio buttons and a check box are added. In the second group box, two radio buttons are placed. In the below section of the form, three buttons are added. Finally, one timer control is added. Then in the form, a group box is added overlap panel. Then, 11 label controls are added to the group box. After that, a progress bar is added. Under the bar, two control panels are added, one high panel and one short panel. In the second (short) panel control, two small label controls are added. Underneath, three button controls are placed. Under these three buttons, a label control is added. For each label control, set the AutoSize property to False to be resized and set (temporarily) the BorderStyle property to FixedSingle so that you can see the edges to facilitate the layout process.

 

In chapter five, you will build Jumper game. In this game, you will move the jumper across the busy road, avoid the tiger, and cross the river with the changing current to get to house safely. You will place four label controls on the top part of the form (set the AutoSize property to False so that it can be resized and the BorderStyle property temporarily becomes FixedSingle so you can see the edges). Then, you use five panel controls below the labels. These panels will be a place for image graphics. Each panel has a width of 16 jumpers or 640 pixels, because one jumper will be given a width of 40 pixels. The first panel will be the jumper house, which will be given a height of 80 pixels. The next panel will become a river, with a height of 120 pixels. The next panel will be a place for tiger, 40 pixels high. Under the snake panel, there is a road panel. This panel will contain three boat lanes. Each boat has a height of 40 pixels, but you will give it a height of 140 pixels (not 120 pixels) to make room for lane markers. The fifth panel is the place where the jumper will begin its journey or leap. This panel will be given a height of 40 pixels. Add the last control panel below the form with three button controls. Then, finally, add four timer controls. Adjust the size of the form so that the panel controls can occupy according to the width of the form.

INTRODUCTION

VISUAL C SHARP CONTROLS

 

 

In this chapter, you will get to know the properties and events of each control in a Windows Visual C# application. You need to learn and know in order to be more familiar when applying them to some applications in this book.

 

 

1.1 Form

Forms are objects where the user interface is designed as shown in Figure 1.1. The form is also known as a container or loader object, because it contains other controls. A number of controls are placed on the form having BackColor , ForeColor , and Font properties. To change it, you can select the desired control (after it is placed in the form) and change the desired properties. Another feature of this container control is that when Enable property is False , all controls on that form will be deactivated. Likewise, when this container control has a Visible property of False , then all controls on the form become invisible.

 

Here, a number of properties, methods, and events commonly used for forms will be presented. Recall that the property describes the appearance and value of a control, a method is an action or task performed by a control, and an event occurs when something is done to that control.

 

Following are the properties of the Form :

 

Table 1.1 A number of properties of the Form object

Name

Used to get or set the form name.

AcceptButton

Used to get or set button that is clicked on form when user presses the ENTER key.

BackColor

Used to get or set the background color of the form.

CancelButton

Used to get or set button that is clicked on form when user presses the Esc key.

ControlBox

Used to get or set a value that indicates whether a control box is displayed on the caption bar of the form.

Enabled

If it is False , all controls on the form will be disabled.

Font

Used to get or set font name, size, and style.

ForeColor

Used to get or set the color of text or graphics.

FormBorderStyle

Used to set form boundaries to be fixed or dynamic.

Height

Form height in pixel.

Help

Used to get or set a value that indicates whether the Help button needs to be displayed or not.

Icon

Used to get or set an icon for a form.

Left

Distance from the left of the screen to the left edge of the form, in pixel.

MaximizeButton

Used to get or set a value that indicates whether the maximized button is displayed on the caption bar of the form.

MinimizeButton

Used to get or set a value that indicates whether the minimized button is displayed on the caption bar of the form.

StartPosition

Used to get or set the initial position of the form when the application is run.

Text

Used to get or set the form window title.

Top

Distance from the top of the screen to the top edge of the form, in pixel.

Width

Form width in pixel.

 

The general syntax for calling a method is to write the name of the control, a dot, and then the method name. For the methods of the Form object, the name of the form used is this . This is a Visual C# keyword that is used to refer to a form. So, to close a form, you use: this.Close () .

 

Following are a number of methods defined for the Form object:

 

Table 1.2 A number of methods from the Form object

Close

Close the form.

Focus

Set the focus on the form.

Hide

Hide the form.

Refresh

Force the form to be displayed again.

Show

Set the Visible property as True .

 

Following are a number of Event procedures that are defined for the Form object:

 

Table 1.3 A number of Event Procedures from the Form object

Activated

Occurs when the form is activated in the code or by the user.

Click

Occurs when the form is clicked by the user.

FormClosing

Occurs when the form is closed.

DoubleClick

Occurs when the form is double clicked.

Load

Occurs when a form is displayed for the first time.

Paint

Occurs when a form is reloaded.

 

General uses of Form objects:

  • Set the Name and Text properties.
  • Set the StartPosition property, for example, to CenterScreen value.
  • Set the FormBorderStyle property to a certain value such as Fixed3D or Sizable .
  • Write down the initialization code needed in the Load event of the form. To access this event in the code window, double-click on the form.
  • Write the finalization code in the FormClosing event of the form.

 

 

1.2 Button

The Button control is probably the most commonly used Visual C# control. This control is used to start, interrupt, or end certain processes. The following will be presented a number of properties, methods, and events for button control.

 

Table 1.4 A number of properties of the Button object

Name

Used to get or set a Button object name.

BackColor

Used to get or set the background color of the button.

Enabled

If it is False , the button becomes visible, but it cannot accept clicks from user.

Font

Used to get or set font name, size, and style.

ForeColor

Used to get or set the color of text or graphics.

Image

Used to get or set the image to be displayed on the button control.

Text

Used to get or set the text or string displayed on the button.

TextAlign

Used to get or set text alignment on Button control.

 

 

Table 1.5 A number of methods of Button object

Focus

Used to assign focus to the button.

PerformClick

Generates a Click event for a button.

 

Table 1.6 The most popular event of Button object

Click

This event is triggered when the button is selected by clicking on it or by pressing the access key.

 

General uses of Button control:

  • Set the Name and Text properties.
  • Write the code in the Click event.
  • You can also change the Font , Backcolor , and Forecolor properties.

 

 

1.3 Label

The Label control is used to display text, which the user cannot edit directly. The text on a label can only be changed when the program is run when responding to an event.

 

The following will be presented a number of properties, methods, and events for label control.

Table 1.7 A number of properties of the Label object

Name

Used to get or set a Lable object name.

AutoSize

Used to get or set a value that indicates whether the label automatically changes size or not. The default value is True .

BackColor

Used to get or set background color on label.

BorderStyle

Used to get or set edge style for label.

Font

Used to get or set the name, style, and size of the font.

ForeColor

Used to get or set the color of text or graphics.

Text

Used to get or set the string displayed on the label.

TextAlign

Used to get or set text alignment on label.

 

Note, by default, label control cannot be resized. To do this, set the AutoSize property to False .

 

Table 1.8 One of methods of Label object

Refresh

Force an update to the content of a Label control.

 

 

Table 1.9 A number of Event Procedures from the Label object

Click

Triggered when the user clicks on a label.

DblClick

Triggered when the user double clicks on a label.

 

Common uses of Label controls:

  • Set the Name and Text properties.
  • Set the Font , BackColor , and ForeColor properties.
  • Set the AutoSize property to False and choose the desired value for TextAlign .

 

 

1.4 Timer

The Timer control in Visual C# can generate events without any input from the user. This timer control works behind the scenes on your project, which results in events with the time interval you set. This event generation feature is very helpful when the screen wants to be updated at regular time intervals.

 

The following will be presented a number of properties and event of the Timer control.

 

Table 1.10 A number of properties of the Timer object

Name

Used to get or set a Timer object name.

Enabled

Used to enable and disable timer. When the value is True , this timer control continues operations until the Enabled property is False .

Interval

Milliseconds (there are 1000 milliseconds in one second) between each Tick event call from the timer control.

 

Table 1.11 One of events of Timer object

Tick

This event procedure is called every interval (milliseconds) when the Enabled property is True .

 

To use the Timer control, you add it to your application like other controls. This control will be placed in the area below the form in the design window.

 

The Enabled property of the timer control is False at design time. You enable a timer in the code by changing this property to True .

 

Common uses of the Timer control:

  • Set the Name property and the Interval property.
  • Write the code in the Tick event.
  • At some point in your application, set the Enabled property to True to start the timer. You can also make it False to stop the timer.

 

 

1.5 TextBox

The TextBox control is used to display information entered at the time of design, by user when the program is run, or by code in the program.

 

Table 1.12 A number of properties of the TextBox object

Name

Get or set the name of the text box.

AutoSize

Get or set a value that indicates whether the height of the text box automatically adjusts when the font in the control changes.

BackColor

Get or set the background color from the text box.

BorderStyle

Get or set the edge style of the text box.

Font

Get or set font name, style, and size.

ForeColor

Get or set the color of text or graphics.

HideSelection

Get or set a value that indicates whether the selected text in the text box control is still highlighted when the control loses focus.

Lines

Get or set a line of text in a text box control.

MaxLength

Get or set the maximum number of characters that a user can type in the text box control.

MultiLine

Get or set a value that indicates whether the text box can contain multi-line text.

PasswordChar

Get or set character to disguise password characters in a one-line TextBox control.

ReadOnly

Get or set a value that indicates whether the text in the text box control is read-only.

ScrollBars

Get or set which scroll bars are displayed without the multi-line text box control.

SelectedText

Get or set a value that indicates the text being selected.

SelectionLength

Get or set how many characters that are selected in the text box.

SelectionStart

Get or set the starting point of the selected text in the text box.

Tag

Stores a string expression.

Text

Get or set the current text in the text box.

TextAlign

Get or set text alignment on text box.

TextLength

Get the length of the text in the text box.

 

Table 1.13 A number of methods of the TextBox object

AppendText

Append text to currentvtext in the text box.

Clear

Clear all text in the text box.

Copy

Copy selected text to the clipboard.

Cut

Move selected text to the clipboard.

Focus

Put the cursor on the specified text box.

Paste

Replace the current selection in the text box with the content of the Clipboard.

SelectAll

Select all text in the text box.

Undo

Cancel the last edit operation of the text box.

 

 

Table 1.14 A number of Events from the TextBox object

Click

Occurs when the user clicks on the text box.

Enter

Occurs when the control receives focus.

KeyDown

Occurs when a key is pressed when the control has focus.

KeyPress

Occurs when a key is pressed when the control has focus.

Leave

Triggered when the user leaves the text box. This is a way to check the content of a text box when editing the text box is done.

TextChanged

Occurs when the value of the Text property has changed.

 

General uses of the TextBox control as a viewer control:

  • Set the Name property. Initialize the Text property with the desired string.
  • Set the ReadOnly property to True .
  • If used to display text more than one line, set the MultiLine property to True .
  • You can also change the Font , BackColor , and ForeColor properties.

 

General uses of TextBox control as input device:

  • Set the Name property. Initialize the Text property with the desired string.
  • If used to display text more than one line, set the MultiLine property to True .
  • In the code, give Focus to the control when needed.
  • Provide the key entrapment code for the KeyPress event that will be discussed in this chapter.
  • Read the Text property when the Leave event occurs.
  • You can also change the Font , BackColor , and ForeColor properties.

 

 

1.6 CheckBox

Visual C# has many controls that give users many choices just by clicking the mouse. These controls are attractive, familiar, and minimize the possibility of errors in your application. You will use a lot of these controls.

 

CheckBox control provides a way to provide a selection of a number of potential choices. CheckBox is used in many Windows applications.

 

Table 1.15 A number of properties of the CheckBox object

Name

Get or set the name of the check box.

BackColor

Get or set the background color from the check box.

Checked

Get or set a value indicating whether the check box is checked.

Font

Get or set font name, style, and size.

ForeColor

Get or set the color of text or graphics.

Text

Get or set the string displayed next to the check box.

TextAlign

Get or set text alignment in the checkbox.

 

Table 1.16 One of methods of CheckBox object

Focus

Move focus to a specific check box.

 

Table 1.17 A number of Events of the CheckBox object

CheckedChanged

Occurs when the value of the Checked property changes, whether via code or when the check box is clicked.

Click

Triggered when a check box is clicked. The Checked property is automatically changed by Visual C#.

 

When a check box is clicked, if there is no check mark there ( Checked = False ), then Visual C# will place a check mark there and set Checked property to True . If clicked and previously there was a check mark there ( Checked = True ), then the check mark will disappear and Checked property will be changed to Flase .

 

General uses of CheckBox control:

  • Set the Name and Text properties.
  • Initialize the Checked property.
  • Monitor the Click or CheckChanged event to determine whether the check box is checked.
  • Change Font , BackColor , and ForeColor properties.

1.7 RadioButton

RadioButton control provides the capability to make mutually exclusive choices from a number of candidate choices. This means that the radio button works as a group, only one button can be selected. The radio button is widely used in Windows applications. Named as a radio button because it looks similar to a button on a transistor radio.

 

Following are a number of properties, methods, and events of the RadioButton control:

 

Table 1.18 A number of Properties of the RadioButton object

Name

Get or set the name of the radio button.

BackColor

Get or set the background color from the radio button.

Checked

Get or set a value indicating whether the radio button is selected.

Font

Get or set font name, style, and size.

ForeColor

Get or set the color of text or graphics.

TextAlign

Get or set text alignment on radio buttons.

 

Table 1.19 A number of Methods of the RadioButton object

Focus

Move focus to the specified radio button.

PerformClick

Generates a Click event for a particular radio button, by simulating a click by the user.

 

Table 1.20 A number of Events of the RadioButton object

CheckedChanged

Occurs when the value of the Checked property changes, whether via a code or when the radio button is clicked.

Click

Triggered when a radio button is clicked. The Checked property is automatically changed by Visual C#.

 

General uses of RadioButton control:

  • Create a radio button group.
  • For each button in a group, set the Name and Text properties.
  • Initialize the Checked property.
  • Monitor the Click or CheckChanged event on each radio button to determine which radio button is clicked.

 

 

1.8 GroupBox

You already knew that check boxes and radio buttons work in a group. The GroupBox control provides a way to group related controls in a Visual C# application.

 

To place controls in a group box, you first need to drag or place GroupBox control into the form. Then, place each control into the group box.

 

The group box affects how the radio button works. The radio buttons on a GroupBox control work as a group, and are not related to the radio buttons on other GroupBox controls.

 

Table 1.21 A number of Properties of the GroupBox object

Name

Get or set the name of the group box.

Enabled

Get or set a value indicating whether the group box is enabled. If it is False , then all controls in the group box will be disabled.

BackColor

Get or set the background color from the group box.

Font

Get or set font name, style, and size.

ForeColor

Get or set color of text.

Text

Get or set the string to be displayed in the title section of the group box.

Visible

If it is False , it will hide the group box (and all the controls it contains).

 

The GroupBox control has a number of methods and events, but all of them are rarely used. You will focus more on the methods and events associated with the controls in the group box.

 

General uses of GroupBox control:

  • Set Text and Name properties.
  • Place the desired controls in the group box.
  • Monitor the events of each control in the group box.

 

 

1.9 PictureBox

Visual C# offers a number of features for graphics. The PictureBox control is one of the main tools in exploiting these features. The picture box control can display graphic files (with various formats) and it can utilize a number of graphic functions and can be used for animation.

 

 

Table 1.22 A number of Properties of the PictureBox object

Name

Get or set the name of the picture box.

BackColor

Get or set the background color from the picture box.

BorderStyle

Indicate the edge style for the picture box.

Height

Heighy of the picture box in pixels.

Image

Set the graphic file to display in the picture box.

Left

The distance from the left edge of the form to the left edge of the picture box, in pixels.

SizeMode

Indicats how the picture is displayed.

Top

Lower edge distance from the area of ​​the form title to the top edge of the picture box, in pixels.

Width

Width of the picture box in pixels.

 

Table 1.23 One of Events of the PictureBox object

Click

Triggered when a picture box is clicked.

 

The Image property specifies the graphic file to be displayed. The five types of graphics files that can be placed in the image box are as follows:

 

Table 1.24 A number of acceptable graphic file types of PictureBox control

Bitmap

An image is represented by pixels and stored as a collection that contains bits. This is the format most commonly used by scanner and paintbrush programs. Format has a .bmp extension.

Icon

A special type of bitmap file with a maximum size of 32 x 32 pixels. This format has the .ico extension. The icon is used to represent Windows applications.

Metafile

A file that stores an image as a collection that contains graphical objects (lines, circles, polygons), not pixels. Metafile has a more accurate resolution than bitmaps when the size is enlarged or reduced. This format has a .wmf extension.

JPEG

JPEG (Joint Photographic Experts Group) is a compressed BMP format that supports 8 bits and 24 bit colors. This format is popular on the Internet and is a common format for digital cameras. JPEG format has the extension .jpg.

GIF

GIF (Graphic Interchange Format) is a compressed bmp format originally developed by CompuServe. This format supports up to 256 bit colors and is also popular on the Internet. This format has a .gif extension.

 

 

 

 

The SizeMode property states how a particular image will be displayed. There are five values ​​that can be given to this property: Normal , CenterImage , StretchImage , AutoSize , and Zoom . The effect of each of these values ​​is as follows:

 

Value of SizeMode

Effect

Normal

The image is displayed at the initial size. If the picture box is larger than the image, there will be free space. If the picture box is smaller than the image, the image will be truncated.

CenterImage

The image is displayed at its initial size, centered on the picture box. If the picture box is larger than the image, there will be free space. If the picture box is smaller than the image, the image will be truncated.

StretchImage

The image will 'fill' the picture box. If the image is smaller than the picture box, the image will expand. If the image is larger than the picture box, the image will shrink.

AutoSize

The opposite of StretchImage . The picture box will change its dimensions to adjust the initial size of the image.

Zoom

Same with StretchImage . The image will adjust so it can be loaded in the picture box.

 

Note that the dimensions remain unchanged for the Normal , CenterImage , StretchImage , and Zoom values. With AutoSize , the picture box will change size. This causes problems when the program runs if your form is not large enough to load the picture box.

 

General uses of the PicureBox control in displaying images:

  • Set the Name and SizeMode properties (often with a StretchImage value).
  • Specifiy the Image property, both at the time of design and when the program runs (run-time).

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

TUTORIAL 1

THROWING FIRE

 

 

In this tutorial, you will build Throwing Fire program. This program can be played by two human players or human player versus computer.

 

Description

Start Visual C# and open the project and press <F5> to run it, you will see:

 

Figure 2.1 Throwing Fire game starts

 

Next, press Options button. Choose One . With one player, you can also choose the level of difficulty of the game, as shown in Figure 2.1.

 

Click OK and then click New Game button. Game will start, as shown in Figure 2.2.

 

The controls of the player are done via the keyboard. Player 1 presses A key to move up, Z key to move down, and S key to throw fire.

 

When you choose Two players from the Options button, this game can be played by two human players. Player 1 presses the same keys, while player 2 presses key K to move up, M to move down, and key J to throw fire, as shown in Figure 2.3.

 

Figure 2.2 User chooses one player and hard difficulty level

 

Figure 2.3 User play against computer

Figure 2.4 Human versus human

 

 

Tutorial Steps

Step 1

You will start building Throwing Fire game project. Start a new project in Visual Basic. Place 12 labels, a large control panel, and three control buttons on the form. In the control panel, place a smaller panel with two group box controls and a button control. In the first group box, place 2 radio buttons; in the second box group, place 4 radio buttons. Add two timer controls to the project. Change the size and position of each control so that the form is now as shown in Figure 2.5.

 

All label controls are used for titles and provide scoring and game information. The large panel ( Panel1 ) is the playing field. Three button controls are used to start / stop a program, set options, and exit the program. One timer control is used to control game animation and another is used to represent the computer's decision process. The second control panel ( Panel2 ) is used to select game options. One group box contains radio buttons which are used to select number of players. A group box contains radio buttons to select the level of difficulty of the game, when playing against a computer. A small button is used to close the options panel. The default properties are set for one-player games with the easiest game difficulty.

private void rdoPlayer_Click( object sender, EventArgs e)

{

    RadioButton ButtonClicked;

    ButtonClicked = (RadioButton) sender;

 

    if (ButtonClicked.Text == "One" )

    {

        lblPlayer2.Text = "Player 2:" ;

        lblInstructionPlayer2.Visible = true ;

        grpDifficulty.Enabled = false ;

    }

}

private void FormThrowingFire_Load( object sender, EventArgs e)

{

    try

    {

        StreamReader fileMasukan =

            new StreamReader(Application.StartupPath +

            "\\bolasalju.ini" );

        NumberOfPlayer = Convert. ToInt32(fileMasukan.ReadLine());

        Difficulty = Convert.ToInt32(fileMasukan.ReadLine());

        fileMasukan.Close();

    }

    catch

    {

         NumberOfPlayer = 1;

         Difficulty = 1;

    }

 

    // Makes form visible so options can be clicked

    this .Show();

    pnlOption.Visible = true ;

 

    if (Difficulty == 1)

        rdoEasiest.PerformClick();

    else if (Difficulty == 2)

        rdoEasy.PerformClick();

    else if (Difficulty == 3)

        rdoHard.PerformClick();

    else

        rdoHardest.PerformClick();

 

    if (NumberOfPlayer == 1)

        rdoOnePlayer.PerformClick();

    else

        rdoTwoPlayers.PerformClick();

 

    pnlOption.Visible = false ;

}

 

Figure 2.11 The project is first displayed with default options

 

Note that you use the default values ​​if the configuration file cannot be opened. Also note that you make the form ( this ) and panel ( pnlOption ) appear before selecting options. You choose the difficulty option first, because this option is not enabled if two players are selected. After the option is selected, the Visible property of the panel returnes to False .

Step 16

You will expand the class definition by adding several methods to help with the animation work. Class methods are used so that objects can do certain jobs. The method is written as a Visual Basic procedure. You will write three methods for the TwoPlayer object, one method that places it on a graphical object, one method that moves it to a new location, and another method that removes it. These three methods are added to the class definition just like the general method when added to the form code file. To add a method to the class description, you choose the name and data type of information that will be generated as a return value. In addition, you specify the arguments required by the method.

 

The Place method places a TwoPlayer object into a graphical object named g (passed as argument):

 

1

2

3

4

5

public void Place(Graphics g)

{

    g.DrawImage( this .MyImage, this .Location);

    this .IsVisible = true ;

}

 

Note the use of the Me keyword to refer to the current object or the calling object. After the object is placed on g , you set IsVisible property to True .

 

The Move method moves a TwoPlayer object to a new location. The arguments needed are g ( Graphics object), bc ( Brush object) to delete the previous location, dx (change in location x), and dy (change in location y):

 

1

2

3

4

5

6

7

public void Move(Graphics g, Brush bc, int dx, int dy)

{

    g.FillRectangle(bc, this .Location);

    this .Location.X += dx;

    this .Location.Y += dy;

    g.DrawImage( this .MyImage, this .Location);

}

 

The object was deleted first. The location is then updated and the object is redrawn.

 

The Remove method removes a TwoPlayer object from a graphical object (using bc brush):

 

1

2

3

4

5

public void Remove(Graphics g, Brush bc)

{

    g.FillRectangle(bc, this .Location);

    this .IsVisible = false ;

}

using System;

using System.Collections.Generic;

using System.Linq;

using System.Text;

using System.Threading.Tasks;

using System.Drawing;

 

namespace ThrowingFire

{

    class TwoPlayer

    {

        public TwoPlayer ()

        {

        }

 

        public Image MyImage;

        public Rectangle Location;

        public bool IsVisible = false ;

 

        public void Place(Graphics g)

        {

            g.DrawImage( this .MyImage, this .Location);

            this .IsVisible = true ;

        }

 

        public void Move(Graphics g, Brush bc, int dx, int dy)

        {

            g.FillRectangle(bc, this .Location);

            this .Location.X += dx;

            this .Location.Y += dy;

            g.DrawImage( this .MyImage, this .Location);

        }

 

        public void Remove(Graphics g, Brush bc)

        {

            g.FillRectangle(bc, this .Location);

            this .IsVisible = false ;

        }

    }

}

 

Using this class, a TwoPlayer object variable can be created using:

 

1

TwoPlayer MyPlayer

 

The variable then is used to reference new TwoPlayer player:

 

1

MyPlayer = new TwoPlayer()

 

Once created, the MyImage property can be specified using Image.FromFile method and the Location property can be assigned a Rectangle structure.

 

TwoPlayer object is placed on a graphical object ( MyImage ) using: MyPlayer.Place (MyImage) . The TwoPlayer object is moved using: MyPlayer.Move(MyImage, MyBrush, dx, dy) , where MyBrush is a solid brush that has the same color as the background color of the graphical object, dx is how far you want to move the object horizontally, and dy is how far you want to move the object vertically.

MyGraphics is the region of graphics used to play game and MyBrush will be used to erase images. Two TwoPlayer objects ( Player1 and Player2 ) represent two throwers. A FireMax constant (you can change it if you like) sets the number of initial pitches each player has.

private void FormThrowingFire_Load( object sender, EventArgs e)

{

    try

    {

        StreamReader fileMasukan =

            new StreamReader(Application.StartupPath +

            "\\bolasalju.ini" );

        NumberOfPlayer = Convert. ToInt32(fileMasukan.ReadLine());

        Difficulty = Convert.ToInt32(fileMasukan.ReadLine());

        fileMasukan.Close();

    }

    catch

    {

         NumberOfPlayer = 1;

         Difficulty = 1;

    }

 

    // Makes form visible so options can be clicked

    this .Show();

    pnlOption.Visible = true ;

 

    if (Difficulty == 1)

        rdoEasiest.PerformClick();

    else if (Difficulty == 2)

        rdoEasy.PerformClick();

    else if (Difficulty == 3)

        rdoHard.PerformClick();

    else

        rdoHardest.PerformClick();

 

    if (NumberOfPlayer == 1)

        rdoOnePlayer.PerformClick();

    else

        rdoTwoPlayers.PerformClick();

 

    pnlOption.Visible = false ;

 

    Player1Rem = FireMax;

    Player2Rem = FireMax;

    lblRemPlayer1.Text = Player1Rem.ToString();

    lblRemPlayer2.Text = Player2Rem.ToString();

 

    // Creates TwoPlayer objects

    MyGraphics = pnlGame.CreateGraphics();

    MyBrush = new SolidBrush(pnlGame.BackColor);

    Player1 = new TwoPlayer();

    Player2 = new TwoPlayer();

    Player1.MyImage = Image.FromFile(Application.StartupPath +

        "\\player1.ico" );

    Player2.MyImage = Image.FromFile(Application.StartupPath +

        "\\plyer2.ico" );

}

 

Pay attention to the code to create two TwoPlayer objects and initialize MyImage property. Copy the player1.ico and player2.ico graphic files into bin\Debug folder.

 

Step 19

At this point, the user can click on New Game ( btnGame ) to start the game. The following steps will be added:

  • Remove all graphic objects.
  • Change the Text property from btnGame to Stop Game .
  • Disable btnOption .
  • Disable Exit button.
  • Reset Player1Hit and Player2Hit to 0.
  • Reset Player1Rem and Player2Rem to FireMax .
  • Place Player1 and Player2 objects to the starting position (using Place method of TwoPlayer class).

 

The code for these steps is quite simple. The Player1 object will be centered vertically on pnlGame near the left edge. The Player2 object will be centered vertically on pnlGame near the right edge.

 

The btnGame button is also used to stop the game. When the user clicks btnGame button (when its Text property is Stop Game ), the following things need to be done:

  • Delete Player1 and Player2 objects (using Remove method of TwoPlayer class).
  • Change Text property from btnGame to Start Game .
  • Enable btnOption .
  • Enable Exit button.
  • Display “Game Over” message.

The code for all of these steps is placed in the Click event procedure of btnGame . The code is given as follows:

private void btnGame_Click( object sender, EventArgs e)

{

    if (btnGame.Text == "New Game" )

    {

        MyGraphics.Clear(pnlGame.BackColor);

        btnGame.Text = "Stop Game" ;

        btnOption.Enabled = false ;

        btnExit.Enabled = false ;

        Player1Hit = 0;

        Player2Hit = 0;

        lblHitPlayer1.Text = "0" ;

        lblHitPlayer2.Text = "0" ;

        Player1Rem = FireMax;

        Player2Rem = FireMax;

        lblRemPlayer1.Text = Player1Rem.ToString();

        lblRemPlayer2.Text = Player2Rem.ToString();

        Player1.Location = new Rectangle(5, ( int )(0.5 *

            pnlGame.ClientSize.Height - 0.5 *

            Player1.MyImage.Height), Player1.MyImage.Width,

            Player1.MyImage.Height);

        Player2.Location = new Rectangle(pnlGame.ClientSize.Width –

            Player2.MyImage.Width - 5, ( int )(0.5 *

            pnlGame.ClientSize.Height - 0.5 *

            Player2.MyImage.Height), Player2.MyImage.Width,

            Player2.MyImage.Height);

        Player1.Place(MyGraphics);

        Player2.Place(MyGraphics);

    }

    else

    {

        Player1.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

        Player2.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

        btnGame.Text = "New Game" ;

        btnOption.Enabled = true ;

        btnExit.Enabled = true ;

        MyGraphics.DrawString( "Game Over" , new Font( "Arial" , 24),

            Brushes.Yellow, 280, 160);

    }

}

 

Add this procedure to your project. Positioning “Game Over” message is obtained by trial and error. Save and run project. Click on New Game button and both players will appear as shown in Figure 2.13.

 

Before quit the game, click Stop Game button to make sure the procedure is working properly and “Game Over” message is displayed, as shown in Figure 2.14.

 

At this point, the user has the option to start a new game, change options or exit the program.

The KeyCode property is a member of the Keys class. There are a number of values ​​for each key that can be pressed. The Intellisense feature of the Visual Basic IDE will provide KeyCode values ​​when needed. In this game, you choose the following keys to control the player's movement and to throw fire (selected from the keyboard):

 

Player 1

private void FormThrowingFire_KeyDown( object sender, KeyEventArgs e)

}

Step 22

In this project, you will give players the ability to throw fire at each other. Fire will be represented by Image object just like player. The only difference here is that when fire is thrown, it moves without user interaction at a predetermined speed and its position is updated by the timer control. And, you need to constantly check if the fire collides with another object. TwoPlayer class does not have properties for speed, or methods that check collisions. So, you need a new class to define fire.

 

You will explain fire using MovingFire class. This class will have a number of properties and methods from TwoPlayer class (using inheritance), plus the speed properties and a method for checking collision. To build this class, you can start from scratch, with all new properties and new methods. Or, you can take advantage of the concept of inheritance in object-oriented programming. Inheritance is a concept where you can build an existing class-based class, by adding its own properties and/or methods. This will save work.

 

You will see how inheritance is used. You will add the collision checking method later. Now, just focus on class properties. Add a class to the project, name it MovinFire . Use the following class code:

    public int XSpeed;

    public int YSpeed;

}

 

This will make all the properties and methods of TwoPlayer class available to the new class ( MovingFire ). Other lines of code add speed properties ( XSpeed , speed in the horizontal direction; YSpeed , speed in the vertical direction). These two properties represent how far the MovingFire will move in a certain direction.

}

 

 

Step 25

Player 1 throws fire by pressing the S key. Player 2 throws fire by pressing the J key. You set a number of rules in throwing the fire. First, you will only allow one fire from each player to be displayed on the screen at a time (no multi pitching). Second, the player cannot throw fire if he runs out of rations. If these conditions are met, when the player throws fire, these steps are carried out:

  • Decrease the remaining fires.
  • Update the remaining fires.
  • Position the fire to the side of the player (in the right of player 1, in the left of player 2).
  • Place fire snowballs on graphic objects using Place method of TwoPlayer class.

}

        Player1.Place(MyGraphics);

}

Step 30

If fire is thrown at or hits a player, another player will get point (a hit). You need a way to check for such collision. Because rectangular region defines moving object here, you need to know what if two rectangular regions intersect. In Visual Basic, this test can be performed using ItersectsWith method of Rectangle structure.

 

To see whether the two rectangular regions ( Rectangular1 and Rectangular2 ) intersect, you need to check the Boolean value of Rectangular1.IntersectsWith (Rectangular2) . If the value is True , then an intersection or collision occurs. If False , then there is no collision.

 

To use it on this project, you will add a method, Collide , to MovingFire class. Open MovingFire.vb file and add the following change:

using System;

using System.Collections.Generic;

using System.Linq;

using System.Text;

using System.Threading.Tasks;

using System.Drawing;

 

namespace ThrowingFire

{

    class MovingFire : TwoPlayer

    {

        public MovingFire ()

        {

        }

 

        public int XSpeed;

        public int YSpeed;

 

        public bool Collide(Rectangle r)

        {

            return ( this .Location.IntersectsWith(r));

        }

    }

}

 

This method has a rectangular structural argument (r) for checking collision on the MovingFire object.

 

As an example of using this method, you can check whether Fire1 collides with Player2 . The resulting Boolean value: Fire1.Collide(Player2. Location) will be True if a collision occurs. If a collision occurs, you need to clear the fire and update the thrower's score.

    // status of fire thrown by player 1

        if (Fire1.Location.X > pnlGame.ClientSize.Width)

            // past the edge of the panel

            Fire1.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

        else if (Fire1.Collide(Player2.Location))

            Player1Hit++;

        if (Fire2.Location.X < 0)

            Fire2.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

        else if (Fire2.Collide(Player1.Location))

        {

            Player2Hit++;

            lblHitPlayer2.Text = Player2Hit.ToString();

            Fire2.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

        }

    }

 

    // Checks game status

    if (!Fire1.IsVisible && Player1Rem == 0 && !Fire2.IsVisible &&

          Player2Rem == 0)

        btnGame.PerformClick();

}

private int ShieldSpeed()

{

    const int SpeedMin = 1;

    const int SpeedMax = 4;

    int Speed;

    Speed = MyRandom.Next(SpeedMax - SpeedMin + 1) + SpeedMin;

 

    if (MyRandom.Next(2) == 0)

        Speed = -Speed;

    return (Speed);

}

 

 

Step 37

The movement of the shield is updated on the Tick event of timGame timer. For each update, for each shield, you need to do these steps:

  • Move shield using YSpeed ​​property.
  • Check whether shield has come out of the boundary of the game field.
  • If shield goes out of the boundary of the game field, do this: Calculate new speed; If the speed is positive, position shield to the top edge of the playing field so that it can move down; If the speed is negative, position shield to the bottom edge of the playing field so that it can move up;
  • After moving or repositioning the shield, check whether the thrown fire collides with it. If there is a collision, remove the fire from the game field.

private void timGame_Tick( object sender, EventArgs e)

{

    // Moves shield

    Shield1.Move(MyGraphics, MyBrush, 0, Shield1.YSpeed);

    if (Shield1.Location.Y < -Shield1.MyImage.Height ||

        Shield1.Location.Y > pnlGame.ClientSize.Height)

    {

        // Recalculates speed

        Shield1.YSpeed = ShieldSpeed();

            Shield1.Location.Y = -Shield1.MyImage.Height;

        else

            Shield1.Location.Y = pnlGame.ClientSize.Height;

    }

 

    Shield2.Move(MyGraphics, MyBrush, 0, Shield2.YSpeed);

    if (Shield2.Location.Y < -Shield2.MyImage.Height ||

        Shield2.Location.Y > pnlGame.ClientSize.Height)

    {

        // Recalculates speed

        Shield2.YSpeed = ShieldSpeed();

 

        if (Shield2.YSpeed > 0)

            Shield2.Location.Y = -Shield2.MyImage.Height;

        else

            Shield2.Location.Y = pnlGame.ClientSize.Height;

    }

 

    // status of fire thrown by player 1

    if (Fire1.IsVisible)

    {

        Fire1.Move(MyGraphics, MyBrush, FireSpeed, 0);

        if (Fire1.Location.X > pnlGame.ClientSize.Width)

            // past the edge of the panel

            Fire1.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

        else if (Fire1.Collide(Player2.Location))

        {

            Player1Hit++;

            lblHitPlayer1.Text = Player1Hit.ToString();

            Fire1.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

        }

 

        else if (Fire1.Collide(Shield1.Location) ||

            Fire1.Collide(Shield2.Location))

        {

            Fire1.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

        }

    }

 

    //status of fire thrown by player 2

    if (Fire2.IsVisible)

    {

        Fire2.Move(MyGraphics, MyBrush, -FireSpeed, 0);

        if (Fire2.Location.X < 0)

            // past the edge of the panel

            Fire2.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

        else if (Fire2.Collide(Player1.Location))

        {

            Player2Hit++;

            lblHitPlayer2.Text = Player2Hit.ToString();

            Fire2.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

        }

 

        else if (Fire2.Collide(Shield1.Location) ||

            Fire2.Collide(Shield2.Location))

        {

            Fire2.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

        }

    }

 

    // Checks game status

    if (!Fire1.IsVisible && Player1Rem == 0 && !Fire2.IsVisible &&

          Player2Rem == 0)

        btnGame.PerformClick();

}

private void FormThrowingFire_KeyDown( object sender, KeyEventArgs e)

{

    if (btnGame.Text == "New Game" )

        return ;

    switch (e.KeyCode)

    {

        case Keys.A:

            Player1.Move(MyGraphics, MyBrush, 0, -PlayerIncrement);

                Player1.Location.Y = 0;

            break ;

        case Keys.Z:

            Player1.Move(MyGraphics, MyBrush, 0, PlayerIncrement);

            if (Player1.Location.Y > pnlGame.ClientSize.Height –

                Player1.Location.Height)

                Player1.Location.Y = pnlGame.ClientSize.Height –

                    Player1.Location.Height;

            break ;

 

        case Keys.S:

            if (!Fire1.IsVisible && Player1Rem > 0)

            {

                SoundThrow.Play();

                Player1Rem--;

                lblRemPlayer1.Text = Player1Rem.ToString();                 

                Fire1.Location = new

                    Rectangle(Player1.Location.X + 

                    Player1.Location.Width, Player1.Location.Y,

                    Fire1.MyImage.Width, Fire1.MyImage.Height);

                Fire1.Place(MyGraphics);

            }

            break ;

 

        case Keys.K:

            Player2.Move(MyGraphics, MyBrush, 0, -PlayerIncrement);

            if (Player2.Location.Y < 0)

                Player2.Location.Y = 0;

        case Keys.M:

            Player2.Move(MyGraphics, MyBrush, 0, PlayerIncrement);

            if (Player2.Location.Y > pnlGame.ClientSize.Height –

                Player2.Location.Height)

                Player2.Location.Y = pnlGame.ClientSize.Height –

                    Rectangle(Player2.Location.X –

                    Player2.Location.Width, Player2.Location.Y,

                    Fire1.MyImage.Width, Fire1.MyImage.Height);

                Fire2.Place(MyGraphics);

            break ;

    }

}

Step 44

You certainly can't always find a partner to play the game. So why not if computer becomes your opponent? In the one player option, this game can make a computer as player 2.

 

For such computer control, you need to develop rules to be used by computer as opponent. There are two approaches that can be taken in writing code for computer opponent. You can use simple logic, which makes it very easy for human to win game. Or, you can write code with very detailed logic, which can defeat the human brain. With detailed logic, it will be harder for human to win the match. In this game, you will take both approaches. You first develop simple logic by playing a random game. Then, you use the difficulty level selected using the Options button to determine how often you use random logic versus how often you use detailed logic. The selected values ​​are as follows:

 

Difficulty Level

Simple Logic (%)

Detailed logic (%)

Easiest

100

0

Easy

75

25

Hard

50

50

Hardest

25

75

 

So, when the Easiest level is selected, you use 100 percent simple logic during the game. When the Hardest level is selected, you use 75 percent of detailed logic (you can't possibly make the computer too smart, because human will always lose) and 25 percent of simple logic. The movement of the computer will be controlled by a separate timer control ( timComputer ). For easier games, you will create a greater value for the Interval property for this timer. This will slow down the computer process. The interval values ​​selected here:

 

Difficulty Level

Interval

Easiest

1000

Easy

750

Hard

500

Hardest

250

 

So at the Difficult difficulty level, the computer moves four times more often than when the Easiest difficulty level is selected.

Step 46

Now, you will write down the rules of the computer game. You will start with a simple random rule. In this rule, the computer will only move up and down in the game field, and occasionally throw fire. The only non-random element added is that the computer can only throw fire if it has at least as many fires as the player has. This is to prevent the computer from throwing all the fires and becoming an easy target for human. The rules used are:

  • Generate a random value from 0 to 4.
  • If the random value is 0, throw fire, if computer has at least as many as the remaining fires owned by the player.
  • If the random value is 1 or 2, move up.
  • If the random value is 3 or 4, make down.

With this rule, fires are thrown one by one in five up or down movements. The computer will move up 2 movements of 5 movements and move down 2 movements from 5 movements.

 

In detailed (smart) logic game rules, you only need to think about how you want to win the game. The smart rule is to throw if other players are "within a certain range". And, avoid human player if he throws fire. In the rules given here, "in range" means that the vertical difference between two players is not more than 80 percent of the player's height:

 

  • If it is "in range" and the computer has at least as many fires as the player has, the computer will throw fire.
  • If the human player throws fire or the computer no longer has the remaining fires, the computer will make a defensive move: If human player is above the computer player, the computer will move down; If the human player is below the computer player, the computer will move up.
  • Otherwise, the computer will make an attacking move: If the human player is above the computer player, the computer will move up; If the human player is under the computer player, the computer will move down.

 

Note that the computer can only throw fire when it has at least as many fires left as the player has. You certainly don't want a computer to run out of fires before a human player.

 

The code for both of these logic is placed in the Tick event procedure of timComputer control. Before writing this code, you need to overcome the problem of how you make computer player throw, move up, or move down. With human as the second player, pressing J key will make player 2 throw, K key pressing will make player 2 move up and pressing M key will make player 2 move down. It would be better if there was a way to make the computer press the same key for the job.

 

Fortunately, Visual Basic has a procedure named SendKeys that can be used to simulate key presses on the keyboard. To press J key, the code is: SendKeys.Send("K") . Therefore, for computer player, you will use SendKeys procedure to implement computer actions.

 

The Tick event procedure of timComputer control which implements computer player logic is given as follows:

private void timComputer_Tick( object sender, EventArgs e)

{

    int i;

    if (MyRandom.Next(100) < RandComputer)

    {

        i = MyRandom.Next(5); // Moves randomly

        if (i == 0)

        {

            if (Player2Rem >= Player1Rem)

                SendKeys.Send( "J" ); // Throws fire

        }

        else if (i <= 2)

            SendKeys.Send( "K" ); // Moves up

        else

            SendKeys.Send( "M" ); // Moves down

    }

    else

    {

        if (Math.Abs(Player1.Location.Y - Player2.Location.Y) <

            ( int )(0.8 * Player1.MyImage.Height) && Player2Rem >=

            Player1Rem)

            SendKeys.Send( "J" ); // Throws fire

        if (Fire1.IsVisible || Player2Rem == 0)

        {

            if (Player1.Location.Y - Player2.Location.Y < 0)

                SendKeys.Send( "M" ); // Moves up

            else

                SendKeys.Send( "K" ); // Moves down

        }

        else

        {

            if (Player1.Location.Y - Player2.Location.Y < 0)

                SendKeys.Send( "K" ); // Moves up

            else

                SendKeys.Send( "M" ); // Moves down

        }

    }

}

using System;

using System.Collections.Generic;

using System.Linq;

using System.Text;

using System.Threading.Tasks;

using System.Drawing;

 

namespace ThrowingFire

{

    class TwoPlayer

    {

        public TwoPlayer ()

        {

        }

 

        public Image MyImage;

        public Rectangle Location;

        public bool IsVisible = false ;

 

        public void Place(Graphics g)

        {

            g.DrawImage( this .MyImage, this .Location);

            this .IsVisible = true ;

        }

 

        public void Move(Graphics g, Brush bc, int dx, int dy)

        {

            g.FillRectangle(bc, this .Location);

            this .Location.X += dx;

            this .Location.Y += dy;

            g.DrawImage( this .MyImage, this .Location);

        }

 

        public void Remove(Graphics g, Brush bc)

        {

            g.FillRectangle(bc, this .Location);

            this .IsVisible = false ;

        }

    }

}

using System;

using System.Collections.Generic;

using System.ComponentModel;

using System.Data;

using System.Drawing;

using System.Linq;

using System.Text;

using System.Threading.Tasks;

using System.Windows.Forms;

using System.IO;

using System.Media;

 

namespace ThrowingFire

{

    public partial class FormThrowingFire : Form

    {

 

        int NumberOfPlayer, Difficulty;

        Graphics MyGraphics;

        Brush MyBrush;

        TwoPlayer Player1, Player2;

        int Player1Hit, Player2Hit, Player1Rem, Player2Rem;

        const int FireMax = 20;

        const int PlayerIncrement = 5;

 

        MovingFire Fire1, Fire2;

        const int FireSpeed = 20;

 

        MovingFire Shield1, Shield2;

        Random MyRandom = new Random();

 

        SoundPlayer MySound;

        SoundPlayer SoundThrow, SoundHit, SoundOuch, SoundGameOver;

        int RandComputer, TimeComputer;

 

        public FormThrowingFire ()

        {

            InitializeComponent();

        }

 

        private void btnOption_Click( object sender, EventArgs e)

        {

            btnGame.Enabled = false ;

            btnOption.Enabled = false ;

            btnExit.Enabled = false ;

            pnlOption.Visible = true ;

            lblInstructionPlayer2.Visible = false ;

        }

 

        private void FormThrowingFire_Load( object sender, EventArgs e)

        {

            try

            {

                StreamReader fileMasukan = new

                    StreamReader(Application.StartupPath + "\\fire.ini" );

                NumberOfPlayer = Convert.ToInt32(fileMasukan.ReadLine());

                Difficulty = Convert.ToInt32(fileMasukan.ReadLine());

                fileMasukan.Close();

            }

            catch

            {

                NumberOfPlayer = 1;

                Difficulty = 1;

            }

 

            // Makes form visible so options can be clicked

            this .Show();

            pnlOption.Visible = true ;

 

            if (Difficulty == 1)

                rdoEasiest.PerformClick();

            else if (Difficulty == 2)

                rdoEasy.PerformClick();

            else if (Difficulty == 3)

                rdoHard.PerformClick();

            else

                rdoHardest.PerformClick();

 

            if (NumberOfPlayer == 1)

                rdoOnePlayer.PerformClick();

            else

                rdoTwoPlayers.PerformClick();

 

            pnlOption.Visible = false ;

 

            Player1Rem = FireMax;

            Player2Rem = FireMax;

            lblRemPlayer1.Text = Player1Rem.ToString();

            lblRemPlayer2.Text = Player2Rem.ToString();

 

            // Menciptakan objek-objek DuaPemain

            MyGraphics = pnlGame.CreateGraphics();

            MyBrush = new SolidBrush(pnlGame.BackColor);

            Player1 = new TwoPlayer();

            Player2 = new TwoPlayer();

            Player1.MyImage = Image.FromFile(Application.StartupPath +

                "\\player1.ico" );

            Player2.MyImage = Image.FromFile(Application.StartupPath +

                "\\player2.ico" );

 

            Fire1 = new MovingFire();

            Fire2 = new MovingFire();

            Fire1.MyImage = Image.FromFile(Application.StartupPath +

                "\\fire1.ico" );

            Fire2.MyImage = Image.FromFile(Application.StartupPath +

                "\\fire2.ico" );

 

            Shield1 = new MovingFire();

            Shield2 = new MovingFire();

            Shield1.MyImage = Image.FromFile(Application.StartupPath +

                "\\shield.ico" );

            Shield2.MyImage = Image.FromFile(Application.StartupPath +

                "\\shield.ico" );

 

            SoundThrow = new SoundPlayer(Application.StartupPath +

                "\\throw.wav" );

            SoundHit = new SoundPlayer(Application.StartupPath + "\\hit.wav" );

            SoundOuch = new SoundPlayer(Application.StartupPath + "\\ouch.wav" );

            SoundGameOver = new SoundPlayer(Application.StartupPath +

                "\\gameover.wav" );

            SoundThrow.Load();

            SoundHit.Load();

            SoundOuch.Load();

 

            btnGame.Focus();

        }

 

        private void rdoPlayer_Click( object sender, EventArgs e)

        {

            RadioButton ButtonClicked;

            ButtonClicked = (RadioButton) sender;

 

            if (ButtonClicked.Text == "One" )

            {

                NumberOfPlayer = 1;

                lblPlayer1.Text = "You:" ;

                lblPlayer2.Text = "Computer:" ;

                lblInstructionPlayer2.Visible = false ;

                grpDifficulty.Enabled = true ;

            }

 

            else

            {

                NumberOfPlayer = 2;

                lblPlayer1.Text = "Player 1:" ;

                lblPlayer2.Text = "Player 2:" ;

                lblInstructionPlayer2.Visible = true ;

                grpDifficulty.Enabled = false ;

            }

        }

 

        private void rdoDifficulty_Click( object sender, EventArgs e)

        {

            RadioButton ButtonClicked;

            ButtonClicked = (RadioButton)sender;

 

            switch (ButtonClicked.Text)

            {

                case "Easiest" :

                    Difficulty = 1;

                    RandComputer = 100;

                    TimeComputer = 1000;

                    break ;

                case "Easy" :

                    Difficulty = 2;

                    RandComputer = 75;

                    TimeComputer = 750;

                    break ;

                case "Hard" :

                    Difficulty = 3;

                    RandComputer = 50;

                    TimeComputer = 500;

                    break ;

                case "Hardest" :

                    Difficulty = 4;

                    RandComputer = 25;

                    TimeComputer = 250;

                    break ;

            }

            timComputer.Interval = TimeComputer;

        }

 

        private void btnOK_Click( object sender, EventArgs e)

        {

            btnGame.Enabled = true ;

            btnOption.Enabled = true ;

            btnExit.Enabled = true ;

            pnlOption.Visible = false ;

        }

 

        private void FormThrowingFire_FormClosing( object sender,

        FormClosingEventArgs e)

        {

            StreamWriter FileOutput = new StreamWriter(Application.StartupPath +

                "\\fire.ini" );

            FileOutput.WriteLine(NumberOfPlayer);

            FileOutput.WriteLine(Difficulty);

            FileOutput.Close();

        }

 

        private void btnExit_Click( object sender, EventArgs e)

        {

            this .Close();

        }

 

        private void btnGame_Click( object sender, EventArgs e)

        {

            if (btnGame.Text == "New Game" )

            {

                MyGraphics.Clear(pnlGame.BackColor);

                btnGame.Text = "Stop Game" ;

                btnOption.Enabled = false ;

                btnExit.Enabled = false ;

                Player1Hit = 0;

                Player2Hit = 0;

                lblHitPlayer1.Text = "0" ;

                lblHitPlayer2.Text = "0" ;

                Player1Rem = FireMax;

                Player2Rem = FireMax;

                lblRemPlayer1.Text = Player1Rem.ToString();

                lblRemPlayer2.Text = Player2Rem.ToString();

                Player1.Location = new Rectangle(5, ( int )(0.5 *

                    pnlGame.ClientSize.Height - 0.5 * Player1.MyImage.Height),

                    Player1.MyImage.Width, Player1.MyImage.Height);

                Player2.Location = new Rectangle(pnlGame.ClientSize.Width –

                    Player2.MyImage.Width - 5, ( int )(0.5 *

                    pnlGame.ClientSize.Height - 0.5 * Player2.MyImage.Height),

                    Player2.MyImage.Width, Player2.MyImage.Height);

                Player1.Place(MyGraphics);

                Player2.Place(MyGraphics);

 

                Shield1.Location = new Rectangle(( int )(0.5 *

                    pnlGame.ClientSize.Width - Shield1.MyImage.Width),

                    MyRandom.Next(pnlGame.ClientSize.Height),

                    Shield1.MyImage.Width, Shield1.MyImage.Height);

                Shield2.Location = new Rectangle(( int )(0.5 *

                    pnlGame.ClientSize.Width),

                    MyRandom.Next(pnlGame.ClientSize.Height),

                    Shield2.MyImage.Width, Shield2.MyImage.Height);

                Shield1.YSpeed = ShieldSpeed();

                Shield2.YSpeed = ShieldSpeed();

                Shield1.Place(MyGraphics);

                Shield2.Place(MyGraphics);

 

                timGame.Enabled = true ;

 

                if (NumberOfPlayer == 1)

                    timComputer.Enabled = true ;

 

                this .Focus();

            }

            else

            {

                timComputer.Enabled = false ;

                timGame.Enabled = false ;

                Player1.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

                Player2.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

                Fire1.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

                Fire2.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

                Shield1.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

                Shield2.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

                btnGame.Text = "New Game" ;

                btnOption.Enabled = true ;

                btnExit.Enabled = true ;

                MyGraphics.DrawString( "Game Over" , new Font( "Arial" , 24),

                    Brushes.Yellow, 280, 160);

            }

        }

 

        private int ShieldSpeed()

        {

            const int SpeedMin = 1;

            const int SpeedMax = 4;

            int Speed;

            Speed = MyRandom.Next(SpeedMax - SpeedMin + 1) + SpeedMin;

            if (MyRandom.Next(2) == 0)

                Speed = -Speed;

            return (Speed);

        }

 

        private void FormThrowingFire_KeyDown( object sender, KeyEventArgs e)

        {

            if (btnGame.Text == "New Game" )

                return ;

            switch (e.KeyCode)

            {

                case Keys.A:

                    Player1.Move(MyGraphics, MyBrush, 0, -PlayerIncrement);

                    if (Player1.Location.Y < 0)

                        Player1.Location.Y = 0;

                    break ;

                case Keys.Z:

                    Player1.Move(MyGraphics, MyBrush, 0, PlayerIncrement);

                    if (Player1.Location.Y > pnlGame.ClientSize.Height –

                            Player1.Location.Height)

                        Player1.Location.Y = pnlGame.ClientSize.Height –

                            Player1.Location.Height;

                    break ;

 

                case Keys.S:

                    if (!Fire1.IsVisible && Player1Rem > 0)

                    {

                        SoundThrow.Play();

                        Player1Rem--;

                        lblRemPlayer1.Text = Player1Rem.ToString();

                        Fire1.Location = new Rectangle(Player1.Location.X +

                            Player1.Location.Width, Player1.Location.Y,

                            Fire1.MyImage.Width, Fire1.MyImage.Height);

                        Fire1.Place(MyGraphics);

                    }

                    break ;

 

                case Keys.K:

                    Player2.Move(MyGraphics, MyBrush, 0, -PlayerIncrement);

                    if (Player2.Location.Y < 0)

                        Player2.Location.Y = 0;

                    break ;

                case Keys.M:

                    Player2.Move(MyGraphics, MyBrush, 0, PlayerIncrement);

                    if (Player2.Location.Y > pnlGame.ClientSize.Height –

                           Player2.Location.Height)

                        Player2.Location.Y = pnlGame.ClientSize.Height –

                           Player2.Location.Height;

                    break ;

 

                case Keys.J:

                    if (!Fire2.IsVisible && Player2Rem > 0)

                    {

                        SoundThrow.Play();

                        Player2Rem--;

                        lblRemPlayer2.Text = Player2Rem.ToString();

                        Fire2.Location = new Rectangle(Player2.Location.X –

                            Player2.Location.Width, Player2.Location.Y,

                            Fire1.MyImage.Width, Fire1.MyImage.Height);

                        Fire2.Place(MyGraphics);

                    }

                    break ;

            }

        }

 

        private void timGame_Tick( object sender, EventArgs e)

        {

            // Moves shield

            Shield1.Move(MyGraphics, MyBrush, 0, Shield1.YSpeed);

            if (Shield1.Location.Y < -Shield1.MyImage.Height ||

                Shield1.Location.Y > pnlGame.ClientSize.Height)

            {

                // Recalculates speed

                Shield1.YSpeed = ShieldSpeed();

 

                if (Shield1.YSpeed > 0)

                    Shield1.Location.Y = -Shield1.MyImage.Height;

                else

                    Shield1.Location.Y = pnlGame.ClientSize.Height;

            }

 

            Shield2.Move(MyGraphics, MyBrush, 0, Shield2.YSpeed);

            if (Shield2.Location.Y < -Shield2.MyImage.Height ||

                Shield2.Location.Y > pnlGame.ClientSize.Height)

            {

                // Recalculates speed

                Shield2.YSpeed = ShieldSpeed();

 

                if (Shield2.YSpeed > 0)

                    Shield2.Location.Y = -Shield2.MyImage.Height;

                else

                    Shield2.Location.Y = pnlGame.ClientSize.Height;

            }

 

            // status of fire thrown by player 1

            if (Fire1.IsVisible)

            {

                Fire1.Move(MyGraphics, MyBrush, FireSpeed, 0);

                if (Fire1.Location.X > pnlGame.ClientSize.Width)

                    // past the edge of the panel

                    Fire1.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

 

                else if (Fire1.Collide(Player2.Location))

                {

                    SoundOuch.Play();

                    Player1Hit++;

                    lblHitPlayer1.Text = Player1Hit.ToString();

                    Fire1.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

                }

 

                else if (Fire1.Collide(Shield1.Location) ||

                    Fire1.Collide(Shield2.Location))

                {

                    SoundHit.Play();

                    Fire1.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

                }

 

            }

 

            //status of fire thrown fby player 2

            if (Fire2.IsVisible)

            {

                Fire2.Move(MyGraphics, MyBrush, -FireSpeed, 0);

                if (Fire2.Location.X < 0)

                    // past the edge of the panel

                    Fire2.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

 

                else if (Fire2.Collide(Player1.Location))

                {

                    SoundOuch.Play();

                    Player2Hit++;

                    lblHitPlayer2.Text = Player2Hit.ToString();

                    Fire2.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

                }

 

                else if (Fire2.Collide(Shield1.Location) ||

                    Fire2.Collide(Shield2.Location))

                {

                    SoundHit.Play();

                    Fire2.Remove(MyGraphics, MyBrush);

                }

            }

 

            // Checks game status

            if (!Fire1.IsVisible && Player1Rem == 0 && !Fire2.IsVisible &&

                Player2Rem == 0)

            {

                SoundGameOver.PlaySync();

                btnGame.PerformClick();

            }

        }

 

        private void timComputer_Tick( object sender, EventArgs e)

        {

            int i;

            if (MyRandom.Next(100) < RandComputer)

            {

                i = MyRandom.Next(5); // Moves randomly

                if (i == 0)

                {

                    if (Player2Rem >= Player1Rem)

                        SendKeys.Send( "J" ); // Throws fire

                }

                else if (i <= 2)

                    SendKeys.Send( "K" ); // Moves up

                else

                    SendKeys.Send( "M" ); // Moves down

            }

            else

            {

                if (Math.Abs(Player1.Location.Y - Player2.Location.Y) <

                   ( int )(0.8 * Player1. MyImage.Height) && Player2Rem >= Player1Rem)

                    SendKeys.Send( "J" ); // Throws fire

                if (Fire1.IsVisible || Player2Rem == 0)

                {

                    if (Player1.Location.Y - Player2.Location.Y < 0)

                        SendKeys.Send( "M" ); // Moves up

                    else

                        SendKeys.Send( "K" ); // Moves down

                }

                else

                {

                    if (Player1.Location.Y - Player2.Location.Y < 0)

                        SendKeys.Send( "K" ); // Moves up

                    else

                        SendKeys.Send( "M" ); // Moves down

                }

            }

        }

    }

}

 

TUTORIAL 2

ROASTED DUCK DELIVERY SIMULATION

 

 

 

In this tutorial, you will build Roasted Duck Delivery simulation. In this simulation, a number of decisions are needed. The basic idea is to read the order by incoming telephone and tell the delivery scooter to go to the location of the order. You also need to make sure that you always provide a roasted duck ready to be transported by the delivery scooter. The delivery area is a 20 by 20 square grid. The more roasted duck is sold, the more profit it gets.

 

Description

The panel control on the left side of the form contains the delivery grid. On the upper right are group boxes with two label controls to display the time or hour and sale results. The computer monitor (in a picture box) displays order and delivery status using a list box and label control. Another group box contains a roasting oven when the roasted ducks are displayed using eight picture box controls. Two button controls on the group box control the operation of the oven. Group boxes under the oven show how many ducks are ready to be delivered and how many are in the delivery scooter (a button control is to load the roasted duck into the scooter). The two button controls beneath are used to start/pause the game and to stop the game or exit the game. In the area under the form there are several timers for controlling a number of aspects in the program.

 

The delivery grid consists of 400 label controls on 20 rows (marked with numbers) and 20 columns (marked with letters). Here, you will learn how to place controls on a form (or panel in this case) using code (when the program runs, not when designing the form). This mechanism can save time designing the form.

 

Before running the program, we will explain how to operate it first. You sell and send roasted duck from 6:00 to 11:00. The time in the upper right corner shows the time. The actual game does not use the actual 5 hours in a single game, but only 15 minutes because the timer parameter adjustment has been made. The order window on the monitor shows what time the order came in, delivery coordinates, and the number of roasted ducks ordered. Orders are also displayed on the delivery grid.

 

In the message on the monitor, you are notified of the current location of the delivery scooter on the delivery grid. At the start of the program, the scooter is in the restaurant (marked with the X symbol on the grid). The group boxes below tell you how many roasted ducks are being burned in the oven and how many are in the delivery scooter. To load a roasted duck into scooter, you need to click Load button. To tell the scooter to move to the delivery location, you click on a specific location on the delivery grid. The scooter will depart for the requested position. When it arrives, the scooter will make a sound and notify the results of the delivery. There are four possible outcomes of delivery: (1) on-time delivery, (2) delayed delivery, (3) insufficient roasted ducks in the scooter to be delivered, or (4) no ordering of roasted ducks at a given location. If you successfully deliver, number of sales will be updated.   

 

Figure 3.1 All controls used in Roasted Duck Delivery simulation

 

You also need to control the roasting oven to make sure there are always roasted ducks available to be delivered. To roast ducks, click Put Into Oven button for each duck you want to roast. When the oven is filled, click on Roast Duck button. You will be notified when the duck will finish roasting. When finished roasting, the sound will play and the roasted ducks are moved to the available area. The Roasted group box always shows how many roasted ducks are available to be loaded into the delivery scooter. You can pause the program by clicking Pause Game button. To start the game again, click on Start Again . To stop the program before 11:00, click on the Stop Game button. After the program has stopped, sales reports will be reported on the sales results form.

 

Run the project (press <F5>). Then, click on Start Game button. Wait a second, the phone will ring signaling the entry of roasted duck orders from a specific grid location. In this example, order comes from grid location N 15 at 6:04. You can see the random position of the duck restaurant at R 3:

 

Figure 3.2 Order comes from grid location N 15 at 6:04

 

You can press Load button to load the available roasted duck (initial value of 8) into the delivery scooter. Then, click on the delivery location (in this example, N 15), as shown in Figure 3.3.

 

While waiting for the delivery scooter to arrive at the delivery location, you need to prepare the duck to be roasted in the combustion oven by clicking Put Into Oven button (several clicks as needed, in this case, 8 roasted ducks are put into the oven). Then click Roast Duck :

 

In Figure 3.4, it can be seen that the delivery scooter has arrived at the delivery location (N 15). In a few moments, other orders also comes and scooter departs for another delivery location.
